First, students who have diligently applied themselves to their study, they deserve their praises and privileges, this may encourage those students and others to study harder to win the rewards and propel towards overall academic gains. Second, this kind of competition we would see in almost every aspect of life, where only the best individuals are rewarded. Students are used to this reality and thrive in the face of fierce competition and enable them to achieve success in later life.

Furthermore, emphasizing improvements encourage all students to be diligent in their student also help students to understand that they need to constantly improve themselves, irrespective of how well they have been or are performing. Students can become used to this reality and thrive in the face of fierce competition, which may enable them to achieve success in later life.

However, students who show progress should also be rewarded. If only a few high-achieving students receive rewards, other students may feel that further effort is futile because they cannot surpass those outstanding individuals. As a result, they may feel overwhelmed and disheartened and lose the incentive to study. Furthermore, emphasizing improvements encourages all students to be diligent in their studies and helps them understand that they need to keep improving themselves, irrespective of their current performance. The constant desire to outdo themselves may benefit students more than the determination to defeat others.
In conclusion, schools should reward both students who achieve the best academic results and those who make progress.

paragraphs: Nowadays, some people claim that public museums and art galleries will become unnecessary as computers allow people to view historical objects and works of art. Personally, I am of the opposite school of thought: viewing an image cannot replace visiting a museum or gallery.

Admittedly, technology provides useful access to culture and history. First, high-resolution images, three-dimensional reconstructions and virtual reality platforms allow viewers to explore masterpieces and ancient artefacts in remarkable detail without leaving home. Louvre museum is an example: art lovers around the world can join online tours to view works of art. This is especially useful for those who cannot afford to travel or have mobility issues; they can still access a vast range of cultural and historical heritages.

However, public museums and art galleries are still necessary. Although technology has improved, online experience cannot replicate the direct sensory engagement of seeing an artefact or artwork in person. Such a visit can evoke emotions and a sense of authenticity that digital images cannot convey. For example, seeing an old artefact up close may make its age and authenticity more vivid than an image can. Furthermore, museums and galleries are vital cultural hubs that symbolize the identity of a region. By bringing visitors and local people together around that history, they can attract tourists and help people bond within the community.
In conclusion, I am firmly convinced that public museums and art galleries are still needed. Visits to these places provide a direct experience of history that technology cannot replace.

paragraphs: Nowadays, some people think that governments should ban dangerous sports, while others think people should have the freedom to do any sport or activity. I am personally of the latter school of thought, provided that certain conditions are met.

Admittedly, one might argue dangerous sports should be prohibited by law. This concern is based on the possibility that even a minor error can lead to a participant's death. Skydiving, for example, can put participants at risk of death, and they need professional skills to do it. In my view, such a ban would not be practical. Firstly, dangerous sports often take place in remote locations such as mountain cliffs, where surveillance and control are minimal. Secondly, an officer cannot follow every individual who wants to join such activities. Therefore, a ban may exist only on paper and may drive these sports underground, making basic safety standards harder to ensure.

Personally, I believe people should be permitted to do any sport as long as they understand the risks and receive sufficient training. If people want to try deep-ocean diving or bungee jumping, they should join a reputable club with appropriate equipment and qualified supervision. Furthermore, beginners should be accompanied by an expert and taught what to do when accidents occur. They can then recognise dangers and respond appropriately. Proper training and precautions make participation safer, although no activity is entirely risk-free.
In conclusion, banning dangerous sports is neither practical nor effective. Freedom to choose under strict conditions of training and awareness is a more realistic approach.

paragraphs: Nowadays, some people favour letting children learn through mistakes, whereas others believe adults should help them avoid errors. Freedom to make mistakes should be encouraged, provided that those errors do not involve serious danger.

On the one hand, those who want adults to prevent mistakes have several reasons. Firstly, most mistakes are avoidable: children need not get hurt by knives, fire or electricity to learn to be careful. Secondly, parents have a responsibility to shield children from harm, and by forestalling such mistakes, they fulfil this duty. Lastly, pre-emptively helping children gives parents peace of mind since they know they have done their best to protect and raise them. They can also teach their child to avoid repeating those mistakes.

On the other hand, those who favour learning from mistakes have their own valid reasons. Parents cannot be around all the time; therefore, children will experiment with new things and inevitably make some mistakes. Furthermore, children who make their own mistakes can learn invaluable lessons that will stand them in good stead later in life. In addition, children who are shielded from everything may grow up overdependent on others, which is an undesirable trait.

In conclusion, it seems to me that allowing children to learn from mistakes could prepare them for the future, provided that parents give guidance on important matters and prevent errors that may derail that future.

paragraphs.text: The bar chart compares carbon emissions from gas, oil and coal in the United Kingdom between 1990 and 2010. The figures are measured in millions of tons.

Overall, emissions from gas rose and became the highest of the three by 2000, while those from coal fell steadily. Oil also ended below its starting level, although it recovered briefly between 1995 and 2000. Coal produced the most emissions in 1990, but gas led by the end.

In 1990, gas was responsible for about 220 million tons of emissions, the lowest figure among the three fuels. Its emissions then climbed to approximately 270 million tons in 1995 and 300 million tons in 2000. They increased more slowly thereafter, reaching around 320 million tons in 2010, the highest level shown on the chart. By contrast, coal emissions declined from about 310 million tons in 1990 to 280 million tons in 1995 and 250 million tons in 2000.

Regarding the other fuel, oil emissions started at approximately 270 million tons and dropped to 240 million tons by 1995. They then recovered to about 260 million tons in 2000 before falling to 240 million tons in 2005 and 210 million tons in 2010. Coal continued its downward trend after 2000, ending at around 190 million tons in the final year.

paragraphs.text: Schools differ over whether history or science and technology should be given greater attention. I believe both should remain in the curriculum because they develop different kinds of knowledge that young people need.

Science and technology help students understand and respond to changes in daily life. Science lessons teach them to ask questions and test explanations, while technology lessons show how tools can solve practical problems. For example, students who learn basic programming might design a simple reminder system for an elderly relative. Creating it would require them to plan, test and improve their idea. These skills can also support future work in healthcare, engineering or digital services. However, the value of science is not limited to earning money: it can help pupils judge information and use new devices responsibly.

History offers a different but equally important education. By studying conflicts and social changes, pupils can understand how their society reached its present position. A lesson about a past war, for instance, can help them consider the decisions that led to suffering and the efforts made to restore peace. They may then appreciate why public institutions and shared traditions matter. Historical knowledge does not replace scientific skills, but it gives students context for discussing civic responsibilities and the lives of people who came before them. This can encourage respect without requiring them to accept every past decision as correct.

In conclusion, science and technology provide methods and skills for solving new problems, whereas history helps students interpret earlier human choices. Since these contributions complement one another, schools should teach both subjects and give students opportunities to connect their lessons.
